---
title: Reading Status
llms-description: "How to read what Steward reports: the verdict glyph, the decisions that need a person or an agent, task states and the per-task progress table, the live block, and the run's history — plus acknowledging and raising an item."
---

## Overview

``` bash
steward status
```

`status` is `tend` with its actions discarded — the same reads and the same
decision, with nothing carried out. So it answers two questions at once: where
the run stands, and what the next turn would do. It takes no lock, spawns
nothing, and writes nothing, which is what makes it safe to run as often as you
like while a tend is in flight.

Every turn also leaves the same snapshot in `status.md` at the top of the
workspace. The two cannot disagree about anything, because they are one
function with two renderings.

The snapshot is three sections, and the order is deliberate: **what needs a
decision**, then **where the run stands**, then **what happened**. Surfacing
what a person has to decide is the whole job, and everything else is context
for it — so the decisions are at the top, in full, rather than under a table of
tasks that are fine.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`status` never *writes* `status.md`. So the file holds the last **tend's**
snapshot and can be a full interval stale; the command is always current. If
you want the live picture, run the command.
:::

## The verdict

The first line is one glyph and a count of who is holding the run:

| | |
|----|----|
| ✅ | `nothing needs you` |
| ⚠️ | something does, and work continues — e.g. `⚠️ 1 needs a person, 2 for the agent` |
| 🏁 | `complete — the results are waiting to be accepted` |
| 🛑 | `nothing is progressing` — either something is blocking, or there is unfinished work and no worker running or about to |
| ⏸ | `paused — nothing new is being scheduled` |

The verdict is **run-level, not item-level**: one blocked worker among twenty
running is ⚠️, because a rule that paints red whenever any single thing is
blocked makes red mean nothing.

🏁 is what a finished run reads as, and it is the reason ✅ is narrower than it
looks. A sweep that did everything asked of it is not *nothing needs you* —
nobody has accepted the results yet, which is the most consequential decision in
the whole workflow. Genuine all-clear is a run that is progressing with nothing
outstanding, a paused one, or one whose acceptance you have already recorded.

## Task states

``` text
6 tasks: 3 complete, 2 incomplete, 1 missing
```

Four states, and they are named for the action they imply rather than as a
taxonomy of log conditions:

| state | means | what a turn does |
|----|----|----|
| `complete` | enough of it has been done | leave it alone |
| `incomplete` | a log exists but is short, errored, cancelled, or still being written | resume it |
| `missing` | wanted, and nothing has run | spawn it |
| `orphaned` | a log exists for something the definition no longer asks for | move it to the archive |

`complete` deliberately covers both a clean task and one carrying errored
samples, because both mean *do not spawn*. Whether those errors matter is a
separate question, and it is the one the decisions section is for.

## Progress

The task-state counts answer *what is left*; they do not answer *how is it
going*. That is a question about samples:

``` text
## progress

| task           | samples | done | running | queued | connections | limit          | score |
|----------------|--------:|-----:|--------:|-------:|------------:|---------------:|------:|
| mbpp@gpt-5     | 500/500 | 100% |         |        |             |                | 0.742 |
| gsm8k@gpt-5    | 318/500 |  64% |      38 |    144 |       22/40 | 61k/200k token | 0.669 |
| gsm8k@opus-5   |   0/500 |   0% |         |        |             |                |       |
```

Two sources fill it, and the split is why it is cheap. The denominators, the
score, and the declared limits come from the log headers, which never change
once a log lands — so they are cached and re-read only when the directory
actually changes. Everything that moves — samples running and queued, how hard
the model pool is working, how much of its limit the leading sample has spent —
comes from each live worker's own socket, concurrently, and costs nothing when
nothing is running.

Columns are present or absent for the whole table rather than per row, so a
settled campaign renders four columns instead of eight. A task whose worker does
not answer promptly is reported from its log rather than held up.

`connections` is the model's pool, not the task's, and under packing that
distinction becomes visible: a pool belongs to the process and to a model within
it, so two tasks sharing a process and a model show the same numbers, because
they are drawing on the same pool.

`limit` shows the leading sample's progress toward whichever limit will stop it
first. `score` is the task's headline metric — and because nothing in an eval log
marks a metric as primary, Steward applies a convention and says which one it
picked underneath the table.

### What is running right now

Under the table sits a small block of figures that exist only while something is
running:

``` text
running now: 3 tasks · 12 refusals · 143 HTTP retries · 6.1 GiB across 3 processes · 2.4 cores, average since start
  Live only: refusals and HTTP retries are recorded in no eval log, so these
  describe the tasks running right now and fall as tasks finish.
```

The caveat is not boilerplate. Inspect records neither refusals nor HTTP retries
in an eval log, so nothing can report them for a task that has finished — which
means every number here **falls** as the run completes, and a refusal count
dropping from forty to zero is work finishing rather than a problem resolving
itself.

Memory and CPU are counted **per process, not per task**, because a packed
worker runs several tasks in one process. CPU is an average over each process's
whole life rather than an instantaneous rate: `status` is a read you type on a
whim, and measuring a rate would mean pausing to watch.

The two halves come from different places and fail apart. Refusals and retries
come from each worker's control socket, which a worker deep in a generate may
not answer within the two seconds `status` is willing to wait; memory and CPU
come from the kernel, which answers either way. So a worker that did not answer
is **counted as such** rather than contributing a zero, and its memory is still
in the total:

``` text
running now: 2 tasks · 0 refusals · 3 HTTP retries · 1 not answering · 6.1 GiB across 3 processes · 2.4 cores, average since start
```

When nothing is running the block is absent, and the startup bound the capture
measured takes its place — a ceiling is the useful figure before there is an
actual, and the actual is the useful one once there is.

## What needs a decision

Everything a turn has to report beyond a number is an **item**:

``` text
## what needs a decision

### needs a person

- gsm8k@opus-5 has stopped making progress after 3 attempts and will not be
  respawned — `stalled:gsm8k@opus-5:3`
- the definition has changed since it was captured — `steward launch` · `drift:9f3a1c`

### for the agent

- 2026-08-26T04-11_gsm8k_bad.eval could not be read as a log (unexpected EOF)
  — `unreadable:2026-08-26T04-11_gsm8k_bad.eval`
```

Items are **grouped by who resolves them**, not by kind, because the first
question a reader has is whether any of it is theirs. Yours comes first,
always.

There is one list, filtered rather than duplicated, so the terminal and
`status.md` cannot drift apart in what they say. Where an item has a command
that resolves it, the command is printed with it.

### The kinds

| kind | what it means | whose |
|----|----|----|
| `stalled` | a task has stopped getting anywhere and will not be respawned. Steward never restarts a failed task on its own — see [Running a Sweep](running.qmd#errors-are-counted-not-fixed) | a person |
| `drift` | the definition file has changed since it was captured, so what is running is not what the file says. Resolved by `steward launch` | a person |
| `degraded` | `_steward.md` could not be parsed, so the turn ran on the settings the last one recorded | a person |
| `orphan_running` | a worker is still running work the definition no longer asks for. Stopping it is not a mechanical act, so Steward leaves it and tells you | a person |
| `unsupervised` | no tend has happened for two intervals, so nothing is keeping the run going. A scheduler cannot report its own absence, so this is computed from the journal rather than raised — and only `status` says it, because a tend saying *nothing has tended* is a past-tense fact stated by the turn that disproves it | a person |
| `timer_drift` | the interval `_steward.md` asks for is not the one that is actually armed. Reaching into your crontab unprompted is not a mechanical act, so Steward reports it rather than fixing it — re-arm to resolve | a person |
| `signoff_ready` | every task is complete and nothing further will run, so the results are waiting to be accepted. Worded as a state rather than an instruction, because there is nothing mechanical left to do | a person |
| `unreadable` | a file in the log directory would not parse as a log. One item per file, so one bad file is not a permanent count | the agent |
| `action_failed` | something a turn tried to do did not work. A single-turn fact that either recurs or does not, so it cannot be acknowledged | the agent |

### An id says when you will hear about it again

Each item's id is chosen so that **what re-arms it is what changes it**:

| kind | id | says it again when |
|----|----|----|
| `drift` | the definition's content hash | the definition changes again — and it clears at relaunch for free |
| `stalled` | the task, plus its attempt count | another attempt is made and also fails |
| `degraded` | when the file was last edited | the file is edited and still will not parse |
| `orphan_running` | the task | never — the condition ends when the worker exits |
| `unreadable` | the filename | per file |
| `unsupervised` | when the timer in force was armed | you re-arm — so an acknowledged silence never covers the next timer's |
| `timer_drift` | both intervals, armed and asked for | you edit the file again, and it clears by arming to match |
| `signoff_ready` | a digest of the **committed manifest's work** — each task's identifier, sample count and epochs | a launch commits different work, so there is a different set of results to accept. Not the definition's hash: editing the file without launching changes no results (that is `drift`, a different question), and a byte-identical file can still enumerate different tasks. Not the identifiers alone either, since a task identifier deliberately does not move when the sample count does — that is what keeps existing logs resumable |

## Acknowledging an item

Some conditions nothing will clear by itself. A definition you edited on
purpose keeps reporting drift; a file that was never a log stays unreadable
forever. Left alone, those turn a decisions list into something nobody reads.

``` bash
steward ack drift --reason "renamed a task arg deliberately; relaunching in the morning"
```

`ITEM` is an item id or any unambiguous prefix of one. The item then leaves
`status.md`, the turn's output, and the verdict — a run whose last open item was
accepted reads ✅ — while the journal keeps the record of who accepted it and
why. A reason is required, because it is the only account of the decision that
survives.

It comes back if the condition changes in a way that matters, which is exactly
what the id table above encodes: acknowledging one edit to a definition does not
acknowledge the next one.

`--by` records who decided. An agent relaying your answer records `human`; one
disposing of something on its own judgement — a file it investigated and found
to be a partial upload — records `agent`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`ack` disposes of a *line in a list*. It changes nothing in the run: no worker
is stopped, no sample is re-run, no log is moved.
:::

### Raising, which is the agent's half of the same thing

``` bash
steward raise drift --note "asked in #evals whether the rename was deliberate"
```

An agent cannot accept a decision that is yours, but its own work on one ends
long before you answer — it noticed the drift, looked into it, and put it in
front of you. `raise` records that, and **closes nothing**: the item stays in
`status.md` and the verdict still counts it, because you still owe an answer.
What changes is that the agent stops being handed the same decision every time
it looks.

Only an item under **needs a person** can be raised, and the command refuses the
rest. Taking something out of the agent's queue without closing it is safe only
because you are going to close it; an agent that could do the same to its own
work would strand it — open forever, and gone from the one list that would have
brought it back.

Without it there is no third state, and an agent supervising overnight either
sees the same item sixty times or starts acking things that are not its to ack.
The note is optional, where `ack --reason` is required: disposing of a decision
owes an account, and handing one off does not.

## What happened

The last section is the run's history — what has been *done* to it, oldest
first:

``` text
## what happened

- `2026-08-26T22:14:03.101Z` launched 12 tasks from evalset.py
- `2026-08-27T01:41:07.338Z` a worker exited (pid 40122) with gsm8k@opus-5 unfinished; it is being tried again
- `2026-08-27T01:52:44.870Z` archived a log — orphaned: logs/2026-08-26T21-08_gsm8k.eval
- `2026-08-27T02:03:19.412Z` accepted by human: the definition has changed since it was captured — renamed a task arg deliberately
```

It is the only place a reader arriving at six can learn that somebody dealt with
something at two, which is why `ack` **moves** an item here rather than hiding
it: *who decided, and why* is precisely what a snapshot cannot carry and used to
be discarded.

It is deliberately **complete** rather than a delta — everything material since
the workspace began, not everything since some mark — which is what keeps the
snapshot stateless. That is affordable only because admission is narrow. The
test is whether something happened *to* the run rather than *as* the run: a task
completing is the run happening, a task retried because its worker died is
something that happened to it. Anything that can occur hundreds of times a night
appears as a count, never as instances.

That test is what decides which worker exits appear here. A worker exits at the
end of every task, so recording each one would put a line here per task that
finished. A worker that exits leaving work the manifest still **wants** and has
not got is the other thing entirely, and it is the single event an overnight
history most needs — by morning the snapshot shows that task running normally,
with no sign of how it got there.

The trailing clause is load-bearing. *It is being tried again* appears only when
the same turn actually started a replacement; a departure on the turn the stall
guard gives up, or on a run already at its width, gets no such promise. And a
worker of a task the definition no longer asks for is not here at all — that
story is the archive line.

## Other renderings

``` bash
steward status --format md   # markdown tables, for relaying somewhere
steward status --json        # the whole state as JSON
```

`--format md` matters more than it looks. The default is aligned monospace
columns for a terminal, which collapse into a line of words the moment they are
rendered as markdown — so anything passing the snapshot on to a person should
ask for `md`.

You can also preview against different settings without changing anything:

``` bash
steward status --max-tasks 24
```

An agent supervising the run reads the same three sections through a different
verb — `steward collect`, which adds the history since it last looked and marks
how far it read. See [Working with an Agent](agents.qmd#its-own-queue).
